Hi Sam / Aurora procurement team —

Following our technical deep-dive last week, attached is our recommended Dedicated capacity plan and SKU rationale for the initial reserved cluster. Summary highlights are below; the full cost/latency spreadsheet is attached (aurora_dedicated_sku_analysis_v1.xlsx).

Quick summary:
- Recommended initial mix: 40% H100-reserve (memory+FP16 heavy RLHF inference / long-context), 50% A100-reserve (balanced memory / throughput), 10% L4-burst (low-latency, cost-efficient short-context endpoints).
- Primary driver: Aurora will run two workload classes — long-context clinical summarization (memory-heavy KV/cache usage) and high-concurrency short prompts for search+chat. Memory headroom is required for the summarization pipelines to avoid KV evictions; H100s provide the simplest path with 80GB+ variants.
- Ops fallback: We propose an automatic fallback policy to compatible A100 variants with prefix caching and quantization profiles pre-tested to limit quality regressions. L4s are used for burst/batch inference where sequence lengths are short and quantization is acceptable.

Key asks from Aurora:
1) Confirm priority between latency vs model fidelity for the clinical summarization path. If fidelity (fewer hallucinations) is absolute, we should bias +10–15% more H100 reserve.
2) Procurement preference for monthly reserved vs 12‑month commitment (pricing delta in spreadsheet).

Next steps: I'll loop in Dev for the ops-level fallback config and Irene for contract language (SLA / reserved capacity windows). If useful, we can run a 48‑hour performance pilot on your test dataset with the proposed mix.

Attachments: aurora_dedicated_sku_analysis_v1.xlsx (spreadsheet), ops-fallback-runbook.md (text)

Hi Sam — answering inline to keep this tight.

1) H100 vs A100 for long-context:
- H100 advantage: larger GPU memory variants and TensorCore fp8 pathways reduce the need for aggressive quantization; this preserves model behavior (less calibration). For 40k peak sequences with KV caches, H100 reduces the risk of mid-request OOMs and expensive cache thrashing.
- A100 option: technically feasible if you shard longer sequences across multiple A100s or rely on KV prefix caching that keeps active context small. That introduces additional engineering (sharded KV assembly, more complicated eviction policies) and can increase per‑request latency.

2) Fallback mechanics:
- No model architecture change required in most cases. We deploy compatible model variants (same weights, different quantization/compilation) and switch runtime kernels. Practically: we prepare an A100-quantized build and an H100-optimized build. Fallback is a config switch + warm cache routing. We recommend running a short regression eval set during pilot to certify deviations.

3) SLA implications with L4 burst:
- Reserved H100/A100 carry standard Dedicated SLOs (99.95% node availability). Burstable L4 capacity is best-effort for overflow; if you move 20% of baseline to burst-only L4, recovery under sustained load will be slower and you may see higher error rates on memory-heavy requests. For short prompt traffic, L4 is fine and cost-efficient.

Operational suggestions:
- Pilot plan (48 hours): run synthetic peak tests with 12k avg / 40k peak sequences, collect eviction counts and p95/p99 latencies; compare H100 reserve vs mixed reserve+fallback scenario.
- Quantization profiles: test 8-bit and 4-bit quantized variants on the dev set and flag any >1% metric degradation.

I'll prepare a short ops-runbook for the fallback switch (attached earlier) and a test harness script for your team.
